methods.scope: Apply a stated or standard relation directly.
Chain several dependent inferences.
Use conservation as a main solution method.
Use a static, steady-state, mass or energy balance.
Exploit invariance or symmetric structure.
Reason from dimensions or dimensionless groups.
Use orders of magnitude, proportionality or approximate models.
Study boundary regimes to constrain a solution.
Choose assumptions and construct a representation of a situation.
Establish a general relation rather than only calculate a value.
Extract trends, slopes, areas or values from a graph.
Fit a relation or estimate parameters from measurements.
Quantify and propagate measurement uncertainties.
Choose apparatus, controls and measurement procedure.
Make or interpret observational measurements.
Identify objects, substances or features using evidence.
Reason with positions, orientations, maps or structures.
Compare explanations and evaluate evidence or limitations.
Find a maximum, minimum or best configuration.
Use numerical approximation or an algorithm to obtain results.

difficulty.definition: Recognize a concept or apply one familiar step, once listed prerequisites are known.
Use a familiar method with a short chain of steps or straightforward interpretation.
Select and combine ideas; nontrivial multi-step reasoning with moderate insight.
Requires substantial insight, model construction or coordination of several concepts.
Requires a major non-obvious insight or demanding synthesis, even for a student who knows the prerequisites.

difficultyReference: Relative to the explicitly listed prerequisites, never inferred solely from contest, round or grade.
rules: Assign a concept only when central to the problem; do not tag incidental story context.
Use the most specific supported concept; derive parent fields for browsing.
Allow multiple concepts and cross-subject prerequisites.
Methods may reveal solution strategy: expose them as an optional facet.
Do not infer difficulty from an index summary. Leave unassessed fields null.
Legacy difficulty labels retain their original grade-relative meaning; they are not calibrated onto the new scale.
New aliases require explicit subject scope and review; prefix matches only produce broader suggestions, not automatic leaf tags.
Classification is stored separately from source transcription and references the source content hash.
Split-part difficulty can be recorded; overall difficulty is a reviewed judgment, not the average of parts.
Use accepted human-reviewed anchor problems before declaring ratings calibrated.
